Military officials from two countries to work on promoting ‘effective’ crisis management after constructive meeting in Washington
US and Chinese defence officials met in Washington for the first meeting of a Crisis Communications and Prevention Working Group established under an agreement announced in September when leaders of the two nations met.
The two sides agreed on the importance of “advancing practical communication measures” to reduce risks between the US and China, according to a Pentagon read-out of the meeting released on Tuesday. The delegates also discussed “additional channels” to promote “effective” crisis management and ways to communicate “expediently and effectively”.

Wang Ning joins predecessors in disgrace as Beijing deepens scrutiny of internal security
A former commander of China’s paramilitary force has been stripped of his senior political advisory roles, sealing a sweep of more than 15 years in which three consecutive heads of the People’s Armed Police have fallen from grace.
The top political advisory body revoked his membership during its closing session, which was presided over by China’s fourth-ranking leader and chair of the CPPCC, Wang Huning, according to Xinhua.
China keeps most investigations within its military secret. Consequently, notices announcing the removal of retired generals from China’s national legislative and political advisory bodies have become an important channel for observing the latest moves.

articles.title_orig: Stock futures mixed after big rally following Democrats' decisive midterm wins
articles.title_zh: Stock futures mixed after big rally following Democrats' decisive midterm wins
articles.content_orig:
The newly elected Democratic majorities in the Senate and the House are planning to pass a flurry of bills as soon as they take the reins next January, CNBC has learned, and are preparing to tussle with an antagonistic President Donald Trump .
Follow CNBC's live coverage of the 2026 midterm election results
The legislative push aims to show a united Democratic caucus taking quick action on the issues they were elected to solve, especially oppressively high costs on everything from gas to groceries.
In their first 100 hours after being sworn in, House Democrats plan to bring to the floor bills reinstating the enhanced health insurance subsidies that expired under the GOP-held Congress, and reversing the Medicaid cuts Trump signed into law last year.
Democrats — likely led by Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), who is poised to become the first Black Speaker of the House in U.S. history — also plan to push forward a bill that would undo Trump's sweeping tariffs and reassert Congress' role in setting import taxes. And they will again vote on legislation to end the Iran war or force Trump to seek congressional authorization to keep it going. Some details of the Democrats' plans had been previously reported by the New York Times.
But Democrats will need to strike a balance between these legislative priorities and a robust oversight and investigatory agenda that the party is mapping out to scrutinize Trump, his family, cabinet and supporters in the business world.
"We haven't evaluated who are going to be the targets of the investigation right out of the gate. We'll have those conversations over the next couple of weeks," Jeffries told CNBC on Wednesday.
"But clearly, things aren't going right for the American people. Capitalism is broken in the way in which it is being experienced by so many working-class Americans and middle-class Americans. We've got to make sure we build an economy, a free market economy, that works for everyday Americans," Jeffries said.
Democrats on the campaign trail for months hammered home a message of affordability . And as corruption emerged as a top issue for voters in the waning months of the election, they tried to connect the Trump administration's perceived bad behavior to Americans' pocketbooks.
Already, prominent Democrats are taking a similar tack as they prepare to assume majorities in both chambers.
Sen. Ron Wyden of Oregon, the top Democrat on the Senate Finance Committee, said in a statement on Wednesday that the panel's top priorities "will be affordability for us, accountability for them."
Wyden said the committee would double down on its efforts to make sure billionaires pay their fair share in taxes, address the "corporate chokehold on our nation's health care system" and reassert congressional authority over trade. He also vowed to target the "special interests" that had cozied up to Trump in the past two years.
"From the banks that helped cover up Epstein's crimes, to insurance companies that are delaying and denying health care to churn a profit, to the pharmaceutical company CEOs that price gouge while enjoying Trump's hand-delivered windfalls, when I am chair, they will be forced to answer to the Senate Finance Committee for their role in hurting the American people and enabling Trump's corruption," Wyden said.
Rep. Robert Garcia of California, the top-ranking Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, has vowed to take on Trump's family, corporate corruption, Department of Homeland Security and Immigration and Customs Enforcement overreach and the handling of files related to disgraced sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
Garcia issued a pointed, two-word statement as results tipped toward Democrats on Tuesday night: "Lawyer up."
And Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., a former chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus and member of the House Judiciary and Foreign Affairs committees, said in a recent interview with CNBC that she believed Democrats should target figures like Elon Musk , as well as cabinet secretaries like Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth , Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr., and Attorney General Todd Blanche .
But she acknowledged the challenges that could come with pursuing a large number of potential targets all at once, especially with a potentially unwieldy and ideologically diverse Democratic caucus.
"I think what we should do is pick one or two cases that really exemplify the worst of the corruption, and that we feel we have the most evidence of wrongdoing," Jayapal said. "There are so many things — I think it's important to focus on a couple."
Meanwhile, other Democrats are angling for some kind of ethics reform package that could include prohibitions on stock trading and use of prediction markets for government officials, a federal ban on gerrymandering and limiting super PAC spending.
"My expectation is that when Democrats are the majority, we will pass a strong bill to ban stock trading in Congress, in the executive branch, and beyond, and that this will be part of a larger package of ethics reforms that we pursue," said Rep. Seth Magaziner, D-R.I., a longtime advocate for such legislation.

articles.title_orig: How India Can Manage Chinese Surpluses
articles.title_zh: How India Can Manage Chinese Surpluses
articles.content_orig:
By Thomas Asplund-Meineckem , William B. Smith, and  Shiro Armstrong
China’s resurgent trade surplus has revived fears across developing Asia that it is pulling up the ladder of export-led industrialization behind it. In New Delhi, India’s bilateral trade deficit with China — over $112 billion in 2025–26 — is being read as the result of unfair Chinese competition and domestic structural weakness, both cited as grounds for protection. But viewing China primarily as a competitor misses its potentially complementary role and the case for managing the relationship rather than retreating from it.
Concerns over a ‘China squeeze’ hold that China has industrialized without ceding labor-intensive industries, partly due to its industrial policies and structurally undervalued renminbi. The argument goes that Chinese goods undercut developing countries’ firms at home and outcompete them in third markets, while China demands few of their exports, leaving developing countries little room to industrialize.
New Delhi has been especially receptive to this argument, framing economic engagement with China as a threat to be contained. In thinly veiled comments directed at China in June 2026, Minister of External Affairs Subrahmanyam Jaishankar argued that ‘the right to industrialize, indeed the capacity to do so, is being denied’ to many developing countries.
Convinced that its firms cannot compete with China on fair terms, New Delhi has turned its trade policy inwards . India has increased tariffs since 2018 to an average of around 17.6 percent, among the highest in Asia, and raised non-tariff barriers. In November 2019, India also walked out of Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) negotiations, largely over concerns it would expose Indian firms and farmers to a surge of cheap Chinese imports. But this ‘ RCEP minus China ’ strategy leaves India outside the regional production networks deeply integrated with China.
Underlying this strategy is concern about India’s bilateral trade deficit. But economies tend to run deficits with countries that supply their inputs and surpluses with those that buy their outputs. Imports of this kind reflect complementarities between economies, and by lowering costs, make local firms more productive and competitive.
China is above all a supplier to Indian manufacturing. Capital goods, machinery and intermediate goods accounted for around 87 percent of Indian imports from China in 2024.
India’s pharmaceutical and electronics industries show the value of integration into Chinese value chains. Between 2015 and 2022, Indian value added in electronics exports nearly tripled as their Chinese content rose sixfold. In pharmaceuticals, it rose by half as Chinese content doubled.
Labor-intensive industries like textiles show a similar pattern. With China moving upstream out of garment assembly, Bangladesh and Vietnam have taken substantial market share. But India’s share of global textile exports has remained stagnant at around 3 percent , with its garment makers paying higher duties on imported fabric.
Tariff and non-tariff barriers to Chinese inputs shelter upstream firms but raise costs for downstream exporters who compete with Chinese exports in foreign markets regardless. Input tariff neutrality would help Indian firms integrate into global value chains, raising domestic value added in absolute terms even if the foreign value-added share of exports rises.
Deeper integration would also help India sell more to China. Despite supplying almost 17 percent of India’s imports in 2025–26, China bought only 4.4 percent of India’s exports. Part of the gap reflects Chinese barriers in key Indian sectors, but Indian firms also struggle to match Chinese rivals on cost and scale.
Indian protectionism against China will not resolve the distortions imposed by Chinese overcapacity . At best, India’s barriers offset some of their effects — but raise costs for Indian firms. India can gain more from importing cheaper Chinese equipment, green technology and productive capacity for its own industrialization — especially given unilateral action will not change the policies driving China’s surpluses.
Genuine Chinese distortions demand a collective response through international and regional agreements. RCEP’s joint committees and ministerial meetings allow members to press Beijing on unfair practices, and its standards and customs chapters provide channels to raise the approval delays preventing Indian goods from reaching Chinese markets.
Membership would also pull India into regional production networks. RCEP’s common rules of origin make it easier to spread production across member economies, since inputs from any member count towards origin, qualifying the final good for preferential tariffs across the bloc. RCEP also provides safeguards against damaging import surges, allowing members to suspend tariff cuts or raise duties when imports injure domestic industries.
RCEP members remain open to India’s accession — New Delhi could take up an observer seat now and apply to join without the waiting period other applicants face. The agreement’s first General Review in 2027 offers a natural moment to negotiate entry.
The Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP) offers further avenues for managing Chinese surpluses. China’s application to join — pending since September 2021 — offers the region leverage, holding out access to CPTPP markets in return for reform of state-owned enterprises, investment and government procurement.
The same logic applies to India, for which CPTPP membership is a longer-term goal. Its regulatory disciplines would demand reforms India’s political economy has long resisted. A staged process — beginning with a gap analysis and cooperation in less contentious areas before negotiating transition periods and carve-outs for sensitive sectors — would give policymakers time to build domestic support for reform.
Indian policymakers should understand China not only as a competitor but as a potential complementor. The trade deficit driving India inwards largely consists of inputs that make its firms more productive and competitive. Unilateral protection and absence from RCEP and CPTPP leave India outside the production networks that would allow its manufacturing sector to prosper, and without a voice to press genuine concerns. Managing the relationship through regional arrangements offers a surer way up the ladder of export-led industrialization than going it alone.
Thomas Asplund-Meinecke is Project Assistant at the East Asian Bureau of Economic Research, Crawford School of Public Policy, The Australian National University.
William B Smith is Project Assistant at the East Asian Bureau of Economic Research, Crawford School of Public Policy, The Australian National University.
Shiro Armstrong is Professor and Director of the Australia-Japan Research Center in the Crawford School of Public Policy, The Australian National University.

articles.title_orig: Russia, China may be more aggressive if they feel Trump is on "his way out": Brookings
articles.title_zh: Russia, China may be more aggressive if they feel Trump is on "his way out": Brookings
articles.content_orig:
Russia and China could become more aggressive over the next two years if they conclude that President Donald Trump is politically weakened and on "his way out" after Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress, Brookings Institution senior fellow Robert Kagan told CNBC.
Speaking on " Squawk Box Asia ," Kagan said the war with Iran had also exposed how Washington has "proved itself rather incapable militarily" in terms of capacity, which would be critical in Asia.
"Everybody can see how much our stocks are depleted in terms of interceptors and missiles, which are of vital interest in the Asian theater," he said.
Congressional Budget Office reports have estimated that the conflict depleted as much as two-thirds of U.S. missile-defense interceptors since June 2025, largely because of efforts to defend Israel against Iranian attacks. This could leave the U.S. with constrained inventories for several years.
Kagan said the deployment of three U.S. aircraft carriers to the Middle East had reduced the U.S. naval presence available in Asia, potentially giving China more room to act assertively in the region.
"I think Trump's only interest right now is in cutting economic deals with China. I don't think he has any real interest in confronting China, but that is going to lead China to be even more aggressive," he said.
In December, Trump approved an $11 billion arms package for Taiwan, but later held back on a second package worth about $14 billion, calling it a "bargaining chip" in talks with China.
China claims self-governing Taiwan as its territory. While Washington does not have a mutual defense treaty with the island, U.S. law requires it to provide Taiwan with the means to defend itself.
Former CIA Director William Burns said in 2023 that Chinese President Xi Jinping had instructed the military to be ready to invade Taiwan by 2027, while stressing that this did not mean Xi had decided to launch an invasion that year or at all.
Kagan's comments come as U.S., China and Russia discuss a possible trilateral summit between Trump, Xi and President Vladimir Putin at the APEC Leaders' meeting in Shenzhen later this month.
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said Wednesday that Beijing was "in communication with relevant parties regarding a meeting between the three heads of state," although no agenda has been announced.
Putin had reportedly floated the idea of a three-way summit with Trump and Xi in October to discuss ending the war in Ukraine, without Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy at the table.
"If it's clear that Donald Trump is on his way out, and the United States may be returning to something like normal, I don't want to overstate that, but they may feel both of them, both Russia and China, may feel that the time to move is in the next two years," Kagan said.

articles.title_orig: China's import expo draws more Fortune Global 500 companies, industry leaders
articles.title_zh: China's import expo draws more Fortune Global 500 companies, industry leaders
articles.content_orig:
This photo taken on Nov. 4, 2026 shows a view of the Hall 3 of the ninth China International Import Expo (CIIE) in Shanghai, east China. (Xinhua/Guo Lei)
SHANGHAI, Nov. 4 (Xinhua) -- The numbers of overseas companies and industry heavyweights attending the 9th China International Import Expo (CIIE) are both set to reach record highs, underscoring the enduring appeal of the world's largest import-themed trade fair.
The event is scheduled to open on Thursday in Shanghai, east China, with more than 300 Fortune Global 500 companies and industry leaders expected to participate, marking a record high. Additionally, more than 2,000 companies will be exhibiting here for the first time, according to organizers.
This year's expo is expected to attract a record 4,142 overseas exhibitors from 148 countries and regions. In total, 162 countries, regions and international organizations will participate, according to the Ministry of Commerce.
Since its launch in 2018, the trade fair has maintained strong appeal for international companies of all sizes, which have used the platform as a launchpad for new products in China and a fast track to enter the world's second-largest consumer market.
Danish pharmaceutical giant Novo Nordisk, which has participated in all the previous eight editions of the expo, will showcase new medicines during this year's event, including Kyinsu, a once-weekly injection for type 2 diabetes.
"The CIIE has become an important part of our work in China," said Mike Doustdar, president and CEO of Novo Nordisk. "This is our ninth consecutive year taking part, and many medicines we first presented at the expo have since launched here."
This year, over 480 exhibits are set to make their global, Asian or China debuts -- another record for the event.
Canada-headquartered athletic apparel brand lululemon will participate in the trade fair for the third consecutive year, with China now serving as its second-largest market globally.
"The CIIE is far more than a platform to showcase products," said San Yan Ng, regional president of lululemon China and APAC. "It also gives us the opportunity to engage in deeper dialogue and build stronger connections with Chinese guests, partners, government stakeholders and friends from all sectors."
The CIIE is a prominent example of China's efforts to open its market wider and facilitate entry of quality products from around the world. China expects the expanded imports will boost domestic demands and support its industrial upgrading.
The nation's imports reached 16.7 trillion yuan (about 2.48 trillion U.S. dollars) in the first nine months of this year, up 22.3 percent, the fastest growth since 2021.

articles.title_orig: UK found to be ‘dangerously’ reliant on China for critical minerals needed for defence and AI
articles.title_zh: UK found to be ‘dangerously’ reliant on China for critical minerals needed for defence and AI
articles.content_orig:
Delivering net zero also at risk, say MPs as they call for centralised policy and funding for mines and diversification
The UK is “dangerously” dependent on China for critical raw materials needed for the military, renewable energy infrastructure and AI, a parliamentary investigation has found.
MPs on the business select committee called for an urgent centralised policy and the creation of a “critical minerals finance facility” to help fund rare earth and other critical mineral mines, and deploy grants, equity and debt to accelerate a diversification programme.
“Critical minerals are the alpha of the new economy,” said the committee’s chair, Liam Byrne. “We cannot rearm Britain, build AI or deliver net zero unless we secure the minerals these technologies depend on.
“Yet 16 years after China first weaponised its chokehold over rare earths, Britain remains dangerously exposed.”
It is the second time in a week that the government’s policy on China has been criticised by Byrne’s committee.
China has a stranglehold on the world’s supply of rare earths and other critical minerals, as well as their refined byproducts that are used in everything from military jets to car-locking systems and consumer products such as fridges and washing machines.
The committee heard that “the processing stage” was where the bottlenecks were, with China dominating the refining of seven categories of minerals, including refined lithium needed for electric vehicles and rare earths used in the fuselage and wings of military aircraft to help withstand temperature extremes.
MPs were told that demand for lithium alone would increase 45-fold between now and 2030, leaving the UK in a high-risk dependency relationship with China.
The demand for rare earths needed for permanent magnets used in military jets and other applications would rise 16-fold in the same period as Britain was seeking to rebuild its military capabilities.
But with China capable of suddenly turning off rare earth supplies, as it did in 2025 , a dependency on Beijing was a strategic vulnerability for the UK economy and national security, the committee found.
Separate restrictions on legacy chips after a row over a Dutch intervention in the China-owned Nexperia left the European car industry “days away” from stoppages last October.
The EU, the US and other countries faced the same risk of supplies of rare earths being cut off by China, and the committee said the UK was not putting enough effort into finding alternative supplies.
Donald Trump secured a one-year reprieve on global export restrictions on rare earths from Xi Jinping in October last year. This was extended to January 2027 after the Chinese president’s recent visit to Washington.
However, the reprieve means the UK is at the mercy of US-China relations, the report suggests.
after newsletter promotion
The most “realistic” solution was for the UK to work closely with G7 partners, the rest of Europe and Indo-Pacific countries, to “aggregate demand” and bring in new suppliers.
The committee said its investigation was frustrated by lack of transparency by the government.
“Parliament has no visibility of the capabilities the government is seeking to protect, the vulnerabilities it has identified, or the projects it is backing to reduce risk,” it said.
The committee has drawn up a 10-point plan that includes: working to identify domestic mining; refining and recycling opportunities and their costs; a strategy to encourage business to reduce procurement from China; a plan to unlock investment; and assess planning and permitting processes that may prove a barrier to mining.
As it stood, the committee said it could not be confident the government could satisfy any of its 10 tests.
“The UK requires new institutional and financial muscle,” it concluded.
A government spokesperson denied it did not have a critical minerals strategy saying it was delivering £400m “to ramp up domestic production and recycling” and forge new international partnerships. “Our strategy also sets clear goals for 2035, including meeting 10% of demand through domestic production and 20% through recycling, with no more than 60% of any critical minerals coming from any single country,” they added.

articles.title_orig: Hong Kong pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong sentenced to 10 years in prison in national security case
articles.title_zh: Hong Kong pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong sentenced to 10 years in prison in national security case
articles.content_orig:
Wong, 30, has been imprisoned since 2020 and is the only activist in Hong Kong prosecuted twice under national security law
Exclusive: Joshua Wong laments city’s fate from inside maximum security prison
Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong has been sentenced to 10 years in prison after earlier pleading guilty to “foreign collusion”, his second conviction under a national security law that critics say has been used to silence political opposition in the city.
Wong, who rose to prominence as the teenage face of Hong Kong’s 2014 pro-democracy demonstrations, submitted his guilty plea in September. He had been accused of working with the exiled Hong Kong activist Nathan Law to urge foreign powers to impose sanctions, blockades or other hostile measures against China.
In his ruling on Thursday, high ​court Judge William Tam ‌described Wong’s actions as “grave in nature”.
He said Wong had visited the US to seek foreign interference ahead of the national security law’s introduction in 2020, and continued to share posts on social media by Law calling for sanctions after it was enacted.
Wong’s role was to “supply his underground support” and “arouse the attention of foreign countries to bolster the cause”, the judge said. He described Wong’s actions as part of a “scheme” to collude with foreign governments.
Tam said Wong’s sentence would run concurrently with the remaining term of his previous national security offence.
After the ruling, Law said in a statement: “It’s incredibly sad to see my friend Joshua Wong suffer another sentencing over his peaceful advocacy work for Hong Kong’s democracy.
“The signal the sentencing sent to the world is that [China] is determined to quash any hopes for freedom and democracy on its soil.”
Amnesty International’s deputy regional director, Sarah Brooks, said: “Today’s sentence is another grim reminder of how Hong Kong’s national security law has become a tool to punish dissent rather than to genuinely protect national security.”
Wong wore a dark blue shirt and thick rimmed spectacles in court, and nodded and bowed as supporters waved. Dozens of people had waited in line outside the court building for the hearing, amid a heavy police presence. A group of international diplomats were also present for the sentencing.
The former student leader is already serving a prison term of four years and eight months – imposed in November 2024 – for conspiracy to commit subversion for his role in an unofficial primary election. He has spent nearly six years in detention and had been due to be released in January 2027.
Wong, 30, gained international attention during the 2014 Umbrella protests , which paralysed the city’s financial centre and galvanised a generation of young people. In October 2014, he appeared on the cover of a Time magazine under the headline: “The Face of Protest”.
When protests erupted in 2019 over a proposed extradition bill, Wong was serving a prison sentence for his role in the 2014 demonstrations. He was released at the height of the protests and immediately took to the streets.
The following year, Beijing introduced a sweeping national security law it said was needed to restore stability to the former British colony, but critics say has been used to target political opposition, dissolve civil society groups and silence independent media.
Wong is the only activist in Hong Kong prosecuted twice under the law and his sentencing on Thursday was criticised by human rights groups and supporters.

articles.title_orig: UK commits to 'time-bound' talks on slavery apology
articles.title_zh: UK commits to 'time-bound' talks on slavery apology
articles.content_orig:
The UK has signed up to "structured, time-bound, inclusive and good-faith" talks that address the "historical harms" of the transatlantic slave trade, Commonwealth leaders in Antigua have said.
The formal conclusions marking the end of the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting, known as the communique, is the joint text setting out what has been agreed.
The 18 page document includes a paragraph in which the leaders "welcome the agreement of the Government of the United Kingdom to engage in a structured, time-bound, inclusive and good-faith dialogue with affected parties addressing the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans and its historical harms".
It comes after Prime Minister Andy Burnham opened the door to a formal apology on behalf of the UK for its role in the slave trade, while ruling out the prospect of reparations.
Officials said the timeframe for the talks would be agreed at a later date, though the Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has suggested they are likely to conclude in around a year.
Asked whether the government might reach the point of a formal apology by the time it hosts the G20 leaders' summit in Manchester next November, Miliband told BBC Newscast : "Broadly speaking, yes."
The rationale among British diplomats in committing to the wording in the communique is to try to offer reassurance that there is a sense of urgency to deal with the issue, even if a date for doing so is not yet confirmed.
This will be determined, sources said, in the "structured dialogue" the UK is promising with countries that have long demanded that the pain and lasting legacies of the slave trade are, as they see it, properly addressed.
Burnham said his "new approach with the Commonwealth" had been "well received" at the summit.
He said it had "been the most successful meeting of the Commonwealth in recent times," adding that "the King's words have resonated powerfully here and we're really pleased with how it's gone".
King Charles III, speaking in his role as Head of the Commonwealth, told the meeting: "The transatlantic trade in enslaved persons still casts a shadow over these islands and other Members of our Commonwealth.
"As I have said before, that shameful chapter of history is one that fills my heart with horror and my soul with the most profound personal sorrow."

articles.title_orig: Israel’s Herzog accepts vote results, opens talks on forming a government
articles.title_zh: Israel’s Herzog accepts vote results, opens talks on forming a government
articles.content_orig:
Netanyahu: letting Arab parties into gov’t will ‘dismantle’ Israel
Israel’s President Isaac Herzog has accepted the certified results of last week’s parliamentary elections and begun consultations with party leaders on whom to task with forming the next government.
The moves on Wednesday dealt a blow to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s efforts to discredit the vote, in which he and his allies lost their majority in the 120-member parliament, while Arab-led parties made historic gains.
“The elections are over. Now is the time to face reality,” Herzog said.
In the October 27 vote, neither Netanyahu’s coalition nor the bloc of his chief rival, opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, secured the 61 seats required to govern. The prime minister’s coalition won 53, while Eisonkot’s got 48.
That leaves open the possibility of an alliance between the two men or an alliance between Eisenkot and the Arab-led parties – Ra’am and the Joint List – which had secured a record 19 seats.
Herzog concluded the first day of consultations with party leaders on Wednesday night, and said talks would continue on Thursday.
On Wednesday, the president said he met with representatives of the Religious Zionism and Zehut, Shas, and Yisrael Beytenu factions. He “received their recommendations regarding the identity of the Knesset member upon whom the task of forming the government should be assigned,” Herzog said on X.
Three factions aligned with Netanyahu’s religious-nationalist base recommended that the prime minister be given a chance to form a coalition, while a fourth, led by a former Netanyahu ally turned rival, backed Eisenkot.
Eight more parties, including the two Arab-led factions, are scheduled to meet with the president on Thursday, with Eisenkot’s Yashar party and Netanyahu’s Likud going last.
Eisenkot’s prospects improved when Ra’am, a major Arab-led party, said it would recommend him. That brought his expected support to 56 lawmakers, according to the Israeli news site Ynet, which is still short of a majority.
The other Arab-led party, the Joint List, has not announced its position. Israel’s Channel 12 reported that the party was expected to coordinate with Eisenkot, endorsing him if asked or abstaining if he preferred. Its 11 seats could push him past 61.
Netanyahu’s 53-seat bloc, by contrast, may not yield 53 endorsements.
Degel HaTorah, which holds four of United Torah Judaism’s seven seats, said it would recommend neither candidate. The ultra-Orthodox faction broke with Netanyahu over his coalition’s failure to pass legislation exempting Haredi men from military service, The Times of Israel reported.
Once the consultations end, Herzog will choose the candidate he considers best placed to assemble a coalition, almost certainly Netanyahu or Eisenkot. He has several days to announce his decision, after which the nominee will have 28 days to form a government, with a possible 14-day extension.
If neither man succeeds, Israel would hold another election early next year.
Netanyahu and his supporters meanwhile have repeatedly made unsubstantiated claims that the Arab-led parties had “stolen” the election, possibly with foreign assistance.
But Israel’s elections commission said earlier on Wednesday that it had conducted a thorough investigation of all parties’ claims of fraud and found “no evidence of irregularities that compromised the integrity of the election or affected its results”.
Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara also rejected a request to question elected officials without supporting evidence.
Herzog urged both camps to compromise to avoid a new election, saying they must accept that “not every commitment and promise can be fulfilled”.
“In the current reality, in which there is no clear winner after the elections, I ask for originality and creativity, courage and goodwill, so that the State of Israel emerges the winner,” he said.
He also backed investigating the suspected interference but warned against smearing Palestinian-Israeli voters, saying he had “great respect” for Israel’s Palestinian minority, which makes up about 20 percent of the population.
“I condemn the coarseness and racist expressions that we have heard recently,” he said.

articles.title_orig: Datacenters were on the ballot. US voters rejected them
articles.title_zh: Datacenters were on the ballot. US voters rejected them
articles.content_orig:
Voters approved nearly every datacenter moratorium that was on the ballot, dozens in total in Tuesday’s elections
Track live results from all 50 states
Send us your questions about the US midterms results and Democrats’ ‘blue wave’
There were three big losers in Tuesday’s midterm elections in the US: Donald Trump, Elon Musk and datacenters.
Datacenters, the facilities full of semiconductor chips that power artificial intelligence and a host of other online products, were on the ballot in elections in at least 40 jurisdictions across 10 states. Voters responded with a strong rebuke of the giant buildings, which have has become a symbol of the tech industry and AI.
In Ohio alone, at least 14 municipalities passed bans or restrictions on datacenter development, including in Sunbury, where Amazon has proposed a $2m datacenter project. In Maine, eight municipalities passed temporary datacenter moratoriums. In Emporio, Kansas, where a 1,000-acre gigawatt-scale datacenter was recently proposed, a ban on high-impact datacenters was approved by voters.
Voters approved nearly every datacenter moratorium that was on the ballot, dozens in total, with one notable exception: Hardwood, North Dakota. The small city of a population of less than 1,000 people voted down a bill that would impose restrictions on datacenter development.
Where datacenters were not explicitly on the ballot, officials who have pushed back against their development were elected. In Texas , Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who secured a historical victory as governor on Tuesday night over her Republican opponent, has promised to impose moratoriums on their construction. She has pledged to implement greater restrictions on and community input into whether datacenters can be built. Towards the end of his tenure, Greg Abbott, her Republican opponent, had also tried to capitalize on anti-datacenter sentiment, demanding an end to electricity subsidies for them. He reversed his previous stance that had welcomed datacenters to the state.
Keisha Lance Bottoms, who became governor of Georgia, and Amy Acton, the newly elected governor of Ohio , have also pledged to implement moratoria on the construction of large datacenters.
Anti-datacenter sentiment has grown in the last few months has become a bipartisan issue. In May, Florida governor Ron DeSantis signed a bill imposing strict regulations on large-scale datacenters. Still, last night’s election solidified the overwhelming opposition to these centers of compute that have come to serve as a stand-in for the ultra wealthy and resource extraction by the AI industry.
“Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” Elon Musk, who poured over $400m into supporting conservative candidates, posted on X.
Analyst Dan Ives said the results of the midterms are a clear sign that the pace of datacenter buildout will start to slow down.

“The biggest worry of the night for tech investors and the AI trade was around the state of Texas where 25%-30% of data center gigawatts and capacity will come from,” he said.

articles.title_orig: Inside CVS’s Decision to Break Up a Healthcare Juggernaut
articles.title_zh: Inside CVS’s Decision to Break Up a Healthcare Juggernaut
articles.content_orig:
CVS Health plans to split into two separate public companies by the first half 2028 in what would be one of the largest corporate breakups in history, the company announced Wednesday.
The move would reverse the company's massive $78 billion acquisition of its insurer, Aetna, and dismantle the vertically integrated healthcare conglomerate it created in 2018. The plan would specifically separate CVS' roughly 9,000 retail pharmacies from its major insurance business and pharmacy benefit manager, Caremark, one of the nation's three largest PBMs.
The decision follows a "comprehensive strategic review" by the company's board of directors, according to a news release . Shares of CVS closed more than 12% lower on Wednesday.
It's a stunning reversal for the healthcare powerhouse, which has spent the last two decades working to turn itself into a one-stop health destination. The move also comes as CVS' aggressive turnaround plan under CEO David Joyner shows substantial progress, with the company pursuing $2 billion in cost cuts, store closures, leadership shake-ups and efforts to rein in Medicare Advantage costs.
But Joyner told CNBC's " Squawk on the Street " on Wednesday that the decision to split is "out of a position of strength," pointing to recovery in Aetna's Medicare business and solid performance in the retail pharmacy.
"So it's all about the strength of the business that affords us the opportunity to make what we think are the right strategic decisions for the future of this company," he later added.
CVS shares have jumped roughly 70% since Joyner took the helm in October 2024, bringing the company's market value to $117 billion.
The two new companies would both be publicly traded.
The insurance and PBM company will retain the CVS Health name and be run by Joyner, while the other company will be called CVS Pharmacy and be led by Prem Shah, who is currently group president of CVS Health. Additional leadership positions and board members will be announced at a later date, CVS said.
Existing CVS shareholders will own stock in both companies after the split. The Financial Times on Tuesday first reported the breakup plans.
The company's pharmacy business raked in $37.66 billion in 2025 sales, while its insurance unit booked $36.29 billion in revenue and the healthcare services segment generated $51.24 billion.
CVS on Wednesday also posted third-quarter earnings and revenue that topped Wall Street expectations. Total sales climbed to $108.40 billion, from $102.87 billion in the prior-year period.
Sales were boosted by year-over-year growth in the company's healthcare benefits and health services segments. Meanwhile, revenue in its pharmacy services business slid from the previous year.
On Wednesday, CVS said it will lump its insurer and PBM with its primary care business Oak Street Health, home visit provider Signify Health and the company's specialty drug business.
CVS also said the split will allow the two companies to experience a "focused strategic agenda" and greater ability to "innovate, adopt technology, increase efficiency," among other benefits.
It's not the first time CVS has weighed splitting the company. In October 2024, CVS engaged advisors in a strategic review of its business and considered breaking up its retail pharmacy and insurance units.
But Joyner told CNBC that the company was "in a turnaround" at that time without the flexibility, cash position or business performance to execute a split.
In an interview, Leerink Partners analyst Michael Cherny said the split shows "the stability of the pharmacy," which has won market share from competitors and is seeing gross margins stabilize thanks to CostVantage, a new pharmacy reimbursement model introduced by CVS last year that the company bills as more transparent.
"This business is a much different business from the one that's been considered three years ago, five years ago, 10 years ago, where there had been a litany of headwinds that the pharmacy just couldn't overcome," he told CNBC on Wednesday.
One potential concern for investors is whether the retail pharmacy will lose its competitive advantage of being directly linked with a PBM, which negotiates drug prices and manages prescription drug benefits on behalf of insurers and employers.
But Joyner told analysts Wednesday that the synergy between the two businesses "are going to be preserved in commercial agreements between the two organizations," adding that "we don't need the integration of an operating structure."
Cherny said the rationale for the split could also extend to the state legislative scrutiny over the company's level of vertical integration.
The potential breakup also comes as pharmacy benefit managers face mounting bipartisan scrutiny in Washington, D.C., and across states. Republicans in Tennessee and Arkansas have passed laws that would ban co-ownership of PBMs and pharmacies. Those have been challenged in court by CVS and other companies.
PBMs have been criticized for opaque pricing practices, their growing market power and potential conflicts of interest when they are owned by companies that also operate insurers and pharmacies.

articles.content_orig:
Authorities in British Columbia say more than one grizzly may have been involved in a bear attack that relatives say left a mother and daughter dead along the province’s central coast
More than one grizzly may have been involved in a bear attack that relatives say left a mother and daughter dead in Bella Coola along the province’s central coast, the Conservation Officer Service in British Columbia said.
The service’s Inspector Jeff Tyre said in a video message that the second body had been found in a search by Royal Canadian Mounted Police and conservation officers on Tuesday afternoon that followed the discovery of the first set of remains a day earlier.
He said it’s “not yet clear if more than one bear was involved,” and any bears captured in the area will be assessed.
Family members of art therapist Jenny Balcarras and her daughter, Selah Reed, had reported them missing on Sunday.
Balcarras' brother, Matthew Balcarras, said Wednesday that his sister was “incredibly strong” and had lived in many difficult, remote places, including Alaska, before moving to Bella Coola on B.C.’s central coast a few months ago.
“She was a beautiful artist and was an inspiration for me and my brothers,” Matthew Balcarras said of his sister.
Authorities have imposed a curfew on the community, about 1,000 kilometres north of Vancouver, as the search for the animal or animals behind the attack continues. If the “offending bear” is captured it will be killed to protect public safety, Tyre said.
A fundraiser set up by relative Mary Melissa Smith said Reed was 20, “with her whole life ahead of her,” while Balcarras leaves behind three young adult children, as well as a grandchild.
Balcarras left behind a son, two daughters and a grandson who now are “faced with the devastating loss of their mother,” while navigating the financial burden of arranging funeral services, Smith said.
The Central Coast Teachers’ Association said on social media that Balcarras had joined their school community as a counselor in August, and she devoted “countless hours to connecting with the students she served and worked closely with teachers and other staff supporting their well-being.”
The attack comes nearly a year after a grizzly attack on a group of 20 elementary school students and teachers in the same area, which left one adult and three children badly hurt.
The animal involved in that attack last November was never captured.
Kim Titchener, founder of Bear Safety & More Inc. based in Calgary, said she was concerned when she saw reports about the women on Facebook hiking groups.
“When I saw that they were missing and in the area that they were missing, my heart just dropped because I just kind of knew this could be a bear attack,” Titchener said.
“This community and area have suffered so much last year,” she said, referring to the grizzly attack on schoolchildren.
Bella Coola is well-known for its large population of grizzly and black bears, and Titchener said it’s common for people in Bella Coola to see bears walking near their homes.
Titchener said there have been “concerning pressures” on bear populations in British Columbia because of the loss of habitat, food stress caused by drought and climate change, setting off more conflicts with people.
“I don’t know if Bella Coola suffered from any drought issues, but certainly other parts of the province of B.C. did,” she said.

articles.content_orig:

NEW YORK, Nov 4 (Reuters) - The dollar retreated on Wednesday but was off its earlier lows after a sweeping victory by Democrats in the US midterm elections removed a source of uncertainty for the market while investors gauged ‌the potential for regulatory changes.
Democrats seized control of both the Senate and House of Representatives on Tuesday, scoring sweeping victories in some ‌Republican strongholds for the first time in generations as tens of millions of voters delivered a sharp rebuke to President Donald Trump.
The outsized win eased concerns about potentially contested ​results, although it brought the prospect of divided government and legislative gridlock between a Republican White House and a Democratic Congress, as the US grapples with the Iran war and an AI boom that has fuelled both economic growth and inflation.
US stocks rallied, with the S&P 500 up about 2%, while crude prices plummeted as investors waited for Washington's next move in the US-Israeli war with Iran.
"It's a risk-on feeling. Maybe we're just seeing a bit of ‌a combination of sell the news, buy the ⁠fact, relief that we're not going to be in a quagmire over rigged election results," said Erik Bregar, director of FX and precious metals risk management at Silver Gold Bull in Toronto.
"Fundamentally, you could still see more of ⁠the AI concerns, given the Democrat positioning on data centers and all. But for the time being, markets are relieved that Trump's not going to fight this, and when we see risk-on across the board, that's broadly dollar negative."
DOLLAR INDEX FALLS, EURO CLIMBS
The dollar index, which measures the greenback against a basket of ​currencies, ​fell 0.25% to 101.60 after earlier falling to 101.21, its lowest since September 30. ​The euro was up 0.21% at $1.1217 after climbing to $1.1272, ‌its highest since October 6.
Despite the political shift in the US, expectations for the Federal Reserve's interest rate path remained largely intact. Markets are pricing in an 81.2% chance for a rate increase of at least 25 basis points from the Fed at its December meeting, according to CME FedWatch, up from 77.4% in the prior session.
PAYROLLS BEAT EXPECTATIONS
The election results largely overshadowed a flurry of US economic data.
The ADP National Employment Report showed US private payrolls rose by 86,000 jobs in October, above the 69,000 estimate of economists polled by Reuters. The report was the latest in ‌a string of labor market data this week, which will wind up on ​Friday with the release of the government's payrolls report.
A separate report from the Institute for ​Supply Management said its non-manufacturing Purchasing Managers Index dipped to ​54.5 last month, down from 54.9 in September. The latest reading was slightly below economists' 54.8 estimate but above ‌the 50 threshold that signifies expansion.
Sterling was up 0.38% at $1.3462, ​after rising to a more than seven-week ​high of $1.3503 ahead of the Bank of England's policy announcement on Thursday. The pound was poised for its sixth straight daily gain, its longest run higher since an eight-session streak that ended on July 6.
The Bank of England is expected to bow to inflation ​pressure from soaring energy costs and raise interest ‌rates, although it may push back against investors' bets that several more increases will follow next year.
Against the Japanese yen, the ​dollar weakened 0.14% to 158.43.

articles.content_orig:
The Dow Jones Industrial Average soared nearly 1,600 points, or 3%, on Wednesday, its biggest gain of the year, as investors digested the impact of the Democrats' sweeping victories in the midterm congressional elections.
Other indexes also jumped, with the broader S&P 500 climbing 120 points, or 1.6%, to close at 7,689 and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index gaining 1.4%.
"Investors are happy to have the midterms out of the way," market analyst Adam Crisafulli, head of Vital Knowledge, told investors in a report. "This was a major source of uncertainty, and putting it in the rear-view mirror removes a key obstacle heading into a very favorable time of year seasonally."
The shifting political winds could affect a range of issues that influence investment returns, from the pace of the data center buildout and cryptocurrency industry regulation to proposals to cap credit card interest rates.
At the same time, Wall Street analysts do not expect the outcome to derail a stock market being driven more by robust corporate profits and solid economic growth than by politics.
"The magnitude of the gains for the Democrats in the midterms does not change too much for the near-term policy outlook, given the party still lacks a filibuster-proof majority in the Senate and President Trump has veto power to block legislation," Stephen Brown of Capital Economics said in a note to investors.
Stocks of solar power companies, dollar stores and hospital owners helped lead the way as Wall Street tried to sort the winners from losers following the widespread losses for Republicans.
Investors, meanwhile, see risks ahead for Mr. Trump's social media company, the artificial intelligence sector and businesses owned by Elon Musk, who donated heavily to Republicans. Trump Media & Technology's stock price fell nearly 25% on Wednesday, while shares of Musk-owned SpaceX and Tesla sank 3.8% and 3.3%, respectively.
Investors also expect the election results to heighten gridlock in Congress, with Democratic lawmakers now in control of both the House and Senate, and Mr. Trump threatening to wield his veto power to block any legislation he opposes.
Political gridlock has historically been good for markets because it limits Congress' ability to pass sweeping tax and spending legislation, reducing the risk of volatility, according to Wall Street analysts.
Meanwhile, stocks have generally performed well following midterm elections. The S&P 500 stock index rose an average of 15.5% in the six months after the last 14 midterm races, dating back to 1970, according to figures from investment firm Edward Jones.
"Economic growth, inflation, interest rates and corporate earnings have historically mattered more to broad investment performance than the party composition of Congress, especially if the president and congressional leadership come from different parties," analysts with the Wells Fargo Investment Institute said in a report.
"We do not expect sweeping policy changes," they added. "More likely, in our view, is a split-government alignment on affordability, energy policy and opportunities from artificial intelligence."
Beyond the Beltway, the midterm electoral results could affect key issues for investors, such as the pace of data center construction, with enormous spending on artificial intelligence helping drive stocks to record highs this year while also raising concerns about a bubble in tech stocks .
"In divided government, the policy implications at the federal level may be limited, but data center policy decisions sit at the state and utility-commission level, making gubernatorial and utility races important alongside Congress, particularly Governor Abbott's loss in Texas," Jeff Buchbinder of LPL Research told investors.
"LPL Research continues to expect the buildout to occur, but strong performances by Democrats in key data center states (and pushback from the 'not in my backyard' folks) may slow it down some, potentially increasing regulatory pressure on AI infrastructure stocks including semiconductors, machinery and power generation," he added.

articles.title_orig: Canada, China Extend Tariff Deal, Aim to Boost Canadian Exports
articles.title_zh: Canada, China Extend Tariff Deal, Aim to Boost Canadian Exports
articles.content_orig:
The federal government announced on Wednesday that China will extend its soon-to-expire tariff-free treatment for some Canadian agricultural and seafood products for another two years.
After Prime Minister Mark Carney's January trip to Beijing, China struck a deal with Ottawa that saw it pause its 100 per cent tariffs on Canadian canola meal and peas, and 25 per cent tariffs on lobster and crab.
That deal, which took effect in March, promised to keep tariffs off those products only until the end of 2026.
"This extension gives farmers, producers and harvesters predictable access to the Chinese market, and it's how we will grow our exports to China by 50 per cent by 2030," International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu said in a statement.
Canada reaches tariff-quota deal with China on EVs, canola
Canadian canola has seen some tough years. This could be one of its best
During that January trip, Carney also got Beijing to cut tariffs on canola seed imports from 100 per cent to about 15 per cent for a period of five years.
Canada is the top global exporter of canola and China is the industry's second-largest market after the U.S.
When he signed that initial agreement, Carney made concessions of his own, agreeing to allow up to 49,000 Chinese electric vehicles per year into the Canadian market with a tariff rate of 6.1 per cent.
'Great relief' in Canada's fishing sector as China lifts lobster and crab tariffs: minister
That brought the tariff on Chinese-made EVs down from the 100 per cent level set by the Trudeau government in 2024. China had hiked its tariffs on Canadian goods in response.
The January deal also saw Canada grant improved market access for certain Chinese steel and aluminum products that are in short supply in Canada and cannot be made by Canadian producers.
The federal government announced on Wednesday that it will also extend its market access for those steel and aluminum products until the end of 2028.

He has worked as a reporter and columnist in London, England, for the Telegraph, Times and Daily Mail, and in Canada for the Ottawa Citizen, Torstar and Sun Media. articles.title_orig: After 3 Months Lost at Sea, Five Survivors Are Rescued on Remote Island
articles.title_zh: After 3 Months Lost at Sea, Five Survivors Are Rescued on Remote Island
articles.content_orig:
Five people, including two children, were rescued this week in the South Pacific island nation of Kiribati after three months drifting at sea in a 20-foot skiff, authorities said. Another four remained missing.
Villagers rescued the group Sunday off Fanning Island in Kiribati, the Australian Broadcasting Corp. reported , after they had drifted an estimated 3,355 miles east from the Federated States of Micronesia.
The U.S. Coast Guard in Guam on Tuesday confirmed that the skiff with nine people aboard had been reported missing after it failed to return to Ruo Island in Micronesia on July 30. The group had been making a one-hour crossing between the islands of Murilo and Ruo at the time, ABC reported.
A 10-day search covering 33,000 square miles followed without any sign of the missing boat or those aboard, it said.
"Incredible and wonderful news these five folks were found and are receiving care," the U.S. Coast Guard told The Associated Press in an email.
"Our profound condolences to family and friends of those who did not arrive with them," the email added.
When asked by the AP what happened to the missing four, the U.S. Coast Guard said it was continuing to gather and confirm information and would reply as soon as possible.
A lawmaker in Kiribati, Kaotitaake Rakoroa, told ABC the survivors were being cared for by a pastor on the island.
Nursing officer Paukin Tororo told the ABC on Monday that all five were severely dehydrated and malnourished. They were put on intravenous drips and were showing signs of recovery.
"They can give a smile face, they show the sign they want to eat," she told the ABC.
The survivors had yet to speak publicly about their ordeal and had requested privacy, the Australian broadcaster reported. ABC said the group went missing after their boat was caught in a storm.
The governor of Micronesia's Chuuk state, Alexander Narruhn, issued a statement Sunday saying he had begun talks with the Kiribati government to bring the survivors home.
"There were nine people aboard the boat that went missing. Thanks be to God for his love and mercy that five of the nine have been found," Narruhn said through an interpreter.
"We continue to pray for their four companions," he added. Narruhn did not immediately respond to the AP's request for comment.
There have been previous incidents where people have become lost at sea among the tiny island chains that stud the Pacific Ocean. An Australian man survived more than two months lost at sea in 2023 with his dog Bella after rough seas damaged their boat and its electronics system. Tim Shaddock, 51, had been traveling from Mexico to French Polynesia, but found himself drifting in the Pacific Ocean for more than two months. Shaddock and his canine companion survived by drinking rain water and eating raw fish that Shaddock caught, he said. They were spotted by a helicopter and rescued in July 2023.
Two American sailors and their two dogs were rescued after five months at sea in the Pacific in 2017. Jennifer Appel and Tasha Fuiaba were discovered 900 miles southeast of Japan by a Taiwanese fishing ship, the U.S. Navy said at the time. The vessel's engine died during bad weather, and they were unable to get to land using the ship's sails. The women said the boat drifted off course, and no ships were near enough to hear their distress calls. Water purifiers and a year's supply of food aboard the vessel kept them alive, the Navy said.
In 2024, three fishermen were stranded on a remote Micronesian island for more than a week . They were rescued after using palm leaves to spell out "HELP" in large letters on a beach.

articles.title_orig: JetBlue raises baggage fees for a second time as jet fuel prices stay elevated
articles.title_zh: JetBlue raises baggage fees for a second time as jet fuel prices stay elevated
articles.content_orig:
JetBlue on Tuesday said it is raising its checked bag fees for the second time in less than a year as the carrier moves to offset rising jet fuel and operating costs.
As of Tuesday, checking one piece of luggage for domestic, Caribbean and Latin American flights for most economy passengers will cost $50, up from $39 for off-peak periods, according to JetBlue. For peak travel periods, the fee will rise to $55, up from $49.
In March, the airline hiked its checked-bag fees by up to $9, citing " rising operating costs."
The airline told CBS News the baggage fee increase "helps us keep our base fares competitive while giving customers the choice to pay for a checked bag only if they need one."
JetBlue also said it encourages customers to add their checked bags to their trips at least 24 hours before departure, enabling them to save up to $15 on the first checked bag.
JetBlue Plus, JetBlue Business and JetBlue Premier cardmembers can check one bag for free for the cardholder and up to three travel companions, according to the airline. TrueBlue Mosaic members may also check at least one bag for free. Mosaic 2, 3 and 4 members each get two free checked bags.
Surging global oil prices this year have sharply pushed up the cost of jet fuel, airlines' second-largest operational cost after labor. The price of jet fuel was $4.41 per gallon on Monday, up from just over $2 per gallon in January, according to Airlines for America's jet fuel price tracker .
Other carriers have also raised their baggage fees this year, including Delta , United and Southwest.
Kathryn  Krupnik contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Israel’s election commission rejects Netanyahu claims of voting fraud
articles.title_zh: Israel’s election commission rejects Netanyahu claims of voting fraud
articles.content_orig:
Move comes after attorney general blocks Shin Bet call to interrogate politicians from Palestinian-led parties
Israel’s election commission on Wednesday confirmed the final results of last week’s vote that stripped Benjamin Netanyahu’s far-right coalition of its governing majority, rejecting claims of mass fraud promoted by the prime minister.
The main challenger, Gadi Eisenkot, said Netanyahu had launched a “pogrom against democracy” in attempting to hold on to power by discrediting valid votes and weaponising security forces against parties led by Palestinian citizens of Israel .
Hours earlier, Israel’s attorney general said she had blocked a demand from the Shin Bet security service to interrogate senior politicians from the Palestinian-led parties because she had not been presented with any evidence of wrongdoing.
“In a country governed by the rule of law, neither citizens nor elected officials can be interrogated without evidence that justifies doing so,” Gali Baharav-Miara said in a statement, after Haaretz reported on the attempt to target four politicians.
Election authorities on Wednesday presented the final results to the president, Isaac Herzog, after rejecting allegations they had been tainted by large-scale foreign interference and voter fraud.
“The review found no evidence of irregularities that compromised the integrity of the election or affected its results,” the Central Elections Committee said in a statement.
The body’s chair, Noam Sohlberg, said some “suspicions” were still under investigation but “they do not cast doubt on the election as a whole or justify delaying the election results”.
When the results were handed over, Herzog denounced racist attacks on Palestinian citizens who had turned out to vote at historic rates.
“I condemn the coarseness and racist expressions that we have heard recently,” he said. “I hold Arab society in Israel in great respect. I value its contribution to the country in every area of life, and its desire to integrate.”
Herzog will play a key role in the formation of the next government by choosing which politician has the first chance to create a coalition. He is expected to name Eisenkot, and the announcement could come as early as Thursday evening.
Late on Wednesday, the Palestinian grouping Ra’am said it would recommend that Eisenkot form the next government. The larger Palestinian grouping, Joint List, has said its priority is removing Netanyahu, so is expected to back Eisenkot as the strongest contender to achieve that.
A former leader of the Israeli military who lost his son fighting in Gaza, Eisenkot has secured the public support of all of the Jewish Israeli opposition parties.
However, negotiations could take weeks and Eisenkot warned of ongoing attempts to undermine trust in the election results. He accused Netanyahu of weaponising the security services against domestic opponents in an effort to hold on to power.
“The employees of the Ministry of Defense, law enforcement and the civil service in Israel are servants of the state, not the king,” he said in a statement. “Woe to anyone who abuses their authority and role for political considerations.”
The Shin Bet chief, David Zini, handpicked for the role by Netanyahu, had ordered the interrogations and sought to classify the investigation as a security file, which would have allowed harsher conditions including barring the politicians from having legal counsel.
Nadav Eyal, an Israeli journalist and commentator, said the public should brace for more extreme attempts to dismiss election results and discredit the leading opposition parties.
“The groundwork is steadily being laid for violence,” he wrote on X. “What you’re hearing breaking right now is the foundation of the legal and governmental orders in Israel.”
Netanyahu presided over a racist campaign targeting Palestinian citizens of Israel – about 20% of the population – and on election day began promoting the unfounded accusations of mass fraud now rejected by election authorities.
Ahmad Tibi, one of the most prominent and effective Palestinian politicians, was reportedly among those the Shin Bet sought to interrogate. He responded to the latest allegations, as news broke of sweeping victories for Democrats in the US midterms, with a swipe at Netanyahu’s fear of democracy.
“[The] attorney general is checking suspicion of ties between the Joint List and Democrats in the US,” Tibi wrote in a social media post. “According to the suspicion, in both cases the same sophisticated method was employed: people arrived in droves at the polling stations, cast a slip, and went home.”

articles.title_orig: 7 worst midterm predictions
articles.title_zh: 7 worst midterm predictions
articles.content_orig:
If you looked at the polling , the ad spending , the campaign messaging , the early-vote turnout , and historic midterm trends, you had a feeling Tuesday would be a good night for Democrats.
All metrics pointed to the fact that voters wanted to punish President Donald Trump over his tariffs and war in Iran. And because the only way for Americans to do that was to vote against Trump’s party, Republicans ended the night by losing at least seven Senate seats and dozens of seats in the House.
Yet Republicans, believing they would overperform polling as they had in 2016, 2020, and 2024, deluded themselves into believing all was well. In fact, a number were so confident they made wild predictions that the party would hold on to their congressional majorities.
The predictions were absurd before the election but are even more hilarious to look at now.
Here are seven awful predictions of the cycle:
Johnson made this prediction on Oct. 29 in an appearance on Fox News:
“Hakeem Jeffries will not have a race for speaker, because Republicans are going to win. I’ll be the speaker in the next Congress. I’ll be administering the oath to some of these people who ran for Congress as Marxists, sadly. We’ll see what happens, but he’s going to have to run. Hakeem wants to remain the leader of the Democrats. He’ll be the minority leader if he wins, but they’re going to hold him hostage for all sorts of things. This is a taste of what’s to come. It’s a harbinger of what’s to come for the Democrat Party.”
Mike Johnson: "Republicans are gonna win. I'll be the Speaker in the next Congress." (Bookmark this) (Also, stay for Ainsley Earhardt's comment at the end of the clip 😆) pic.twitter.com/jNIk9R0ojZ
Turns out, Johnson will not be swearing any members in—and he won’t even have a leadership role in the next Congress.
The Daily Mail published a barn burner of an article about the chaos at the White House on Election Day. Nestled in the piece is this gem about what Wiles and LaCivita had been telling Trump in the lead up to Election Day:
As recently as September, the source said, Wiles was telling people directly that Republicans were going to take the midterms.
The source also described weekly Thursday briefings at which veteran GOP political consultant Chris LaCivita, a key Wiles ally, would promise the President that the win was his.
On Tuesday morning, staffers in the West Wing were still talking about picking up seats in both chambers.
‘Delusional,’ the source said. ‘They were delusional right until the very end.’
Blair was one of the masterminds behind Republicans’ efforts to gerrymander their way to a House majority. And after the gerrymandering wars ended, he wrote this in May in a post on X: “Two weeks ago people were dooming and asking wAs rEdIsTrIcTiNg wOrTh iT? …16 net seat swing to GOP…”
Well, as of press time, it appears that only one Democratic-held district that Blair helped target with mid-decade redraws flipped.
In fact, the gerrymander North Carolina passed seems to be a dummymander, with Democrats winning more seats in the state than they had under the old map.
After Tuesday’s elections, House Democrats mocked Blair’s old tweet.
Dems have near them a poster board with a James Blair tweet—the architect of the GOP redistricting push that appears to have backfired pic.twitter.com/UDH61bRFWJ
“53 & 219,” Martin wrote in a post on X, referring to Republicans winning 53 Senate seats and 219 in the House. “Take it to the bank.”
Wonder how much he lost on that bet!
“Texas is turning blue like I’m losing my seat,” Miller texted New York Times reporter Annie Karni in July, when she asked him about the state of his race after being accused of domestic violence .
“You’re better than this,” he added.
Well, Miller lost , and Texas turned blue up and down the ballot.
“For all the panicans…. It’s a red sweep in the senate I’m convinced,” Santos, the disgraced former Republican congressman, wrote just after 10 AM ET on Election Day.
He also made this promise: “If Ohio goes Blue for the Gov and Senator race I’m dressing in drag and doing a cold plunge! Bookmark this!”
Guess we’re getting a show.
Any media outlets using betting sites to influence their election forecasts should be named and shamed.
Bettors on morally bankrupt sites like Polymarket, where you can place bets on sick things like military strikes in Iran, do not know anything besides the vibes they get from reading the news and social media. For example, Kalshi bettors did not predict the races correctly . And they probably lost a boatload of money, too.

articles.title_orig: White House panel delays hearing on Fed's Lisa Cook to Dec. 14
articles.title_zh: White House panel delays hearing on Fed's Lisa Cook to Dec. 14
articles.content_orig:
A White House committee of inquiry postponed from Thursday to Dec. 14 a hearing with Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook for an investigation of whether allegations of false statements in mortgage applications warrant her firing by President Donald Trump , a White House official said Wednesday evening.
But it was unclear if Cook, whom Trump unsuccessfully tried to fire in August 2025, would agree to attend.
The official said the postponement came at the request of Cook.
Her lawyer Abbe Lowell last month said questions about the committee's fairness and objectivity would have to be addressed before the hearing could occur.
Lowell also said the hearing could not take place until December, at the earliest, because she "will be executing her official duties as Governor at financial and monetary policy meetings in Europe."
The New York Times first reported the hearing's rescheduling.
Trump in early October established the committee to investigate allegations that Cook made false statements related to "one or more mortgage instruments."
"The Committee shall investigate the allegations against Governor Cook and report to me whether there is 'cause' for Governor Cook's removal within the meaning of" a federal law that was cited in a Supreme Court ruling in June that temporarily blocked her firing.
The committee is comprised of Kevin Hassett, assistant to the president for economic policy, Andrea Lucas, the chair of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, and Office of Government Ethics Director Keith Sonderling.
Cook has denied any wrongdoing.
In a lawsuit challenging her firing, she argued that Trump's claim about the mortgage statements is pretextual, and that his real reason for trying to oust her is her refusal to agree to his demands that she vote for lower interest rates.
Trump created the panel more than three months after the Supreme Court ruled that the president, for now, could not fire Cook from the central bank's board.
The ruling kept in place a lower court's order preventing Cook from being terminated while the suit challenging her dismissal proceeds.
The decision did not determine whether Trump ultimately has the power to fire a Fed board member. But it said she could remain on the board as her suit was pending because she was not given due process to challenge her firing.
The committee of inquiry Trump set up may be designed to show the Supreme Court that Cook has now received due process.
CNBC has requested comment from Lowell.

articles.title_orig: Mother and daughter die after suspected grizzly bear attack in Canada
articles.title_zh: Mother and daughter die after suspected grizzly bear attack in Canada
articles.content_orig:
Conservation officers say more than one bear may have been involved in attack on women near their home
Search teams in Canada have discovered the body of a 20-year-old woman and confirmed that both she and her mother were killed in an attack that conservation officers now believe could have involved multiple grizzly bears.
Late on Tuesday, conservation officers in British Columbia said the two women, who were reported missing over the weekend, were located near a trail a short distance from their home.
The discovery has shaken a community where, earlier in the year, a grizzly attacked a group of schoolchildren and their teachers.
“Our thoughts are with the families of the victims during this tragic time,” Inspector Jeff Tyre of the British Columbia Conservation Officer Service said in a video posted online. Tyre later said the conservation service was investigating the possibility that more than one bear was involved in the fatal attack.
“We appreciate people’s concerns and the desire to assist but it is critical the public stay out of the area – both due to the danger and to allow officers to do their work,” he said.
Jenny Balcarras, an art therapist, and her daughter Selah Reed were reported missing by relatives over the weekend. A family member posted on Facebook about them, later updating it after the conservation service announced the suspected attack to indicate that their vehicle had been found at a trailhead near Bella Coola, British Columbia. Balcarras’s remains were found first and Reed was located a day later.
A fundraiser for Balcarras started by her family mourned a woman who had recently moved to Bella Coola, a community of roughly 2,100 people, for a new job and “to start a new chapter” of her life. She leaves behind three adult children and a grandchild.
“[Jenny] was working toward building a future and had not yet had the opportunity to establish savings or put aside funds to help her family with unexpected expenses such as these,” wrote relative Mary Melissa Smith. “Tragically, no one could have anticipated that her family would be faced with such an unimaginable loss.”
The family also mourned 20-year-old Selah, who had her “whole life ahead of her” before the attack.
“She was only beginning her journey into adulthood, making this loss even more heartbreaking,” wrote Smith.
Both Balcarras and Reed had lived in communities in remote and rugged parts of the province, as well as time in Alaska.
The suspected attack happened at the Snooka West trail area, about 8km (5 miles) east of Bella Coola, on the province’s central coast.
Bella Coola, which sits at the end of a fjord along the province’s central coast, is a remote location, and abundant food sources mean that grizzly bears are a common sight in the region, which is informally known as the Great Bear rainforest.
Grizzly attacks in the province are exceedingly rare, but last November, 11 people, some as young as nine years old, were injured when a grizzly emerged from the forest near 4 Mile, a Nuxalk community, and attacked a school group on a lunch break alongside a walking trail. Despite an extensive search, the bear was never located.
Samuel Schooner, elected chief of the Nuxalk Nation, said on Tuesday: “Our thoughts are with the victim’s family as they learn of this tragic event.” Schooner said a trapping effort to find the bear was under way and asked media to refrain from contacting community members.
