articles.title_orig: Business Leaders React As a 'Blunami' Sweeps America on Election Night
articles.title_zh: Business Leaders React As a 'Blunami' Sweeps America on Election Night
articles.content_orig:
The 2026 midterm elections delivered shocking wins for Democrats on Tuesday evening, reshaping the balance of power in Washington.
Business leaders, tech executives, and investors are now assessing what the new political landscape could mean for their industries as Democratic candidates flipped key Senate and House seats.
This includes Texas, where James Talarico won his Senate race despite over $150 million in funding from Elon Musk for his Republican rival, Ken Paxton.
After the results, some of the tech and business leaders who sought closer ties with President Donald Trump ahead of his return to the White House could face new congressional scrutiny.
In California, the results of the nation's first-ever ballot measure to impose a one-time 5% wealth tax on residents with net worth exceeding $1 billion could have major implications for the state's elite, though as of around 7 a.m. ET, the "No" vote held a strong lead.
Here's how powerbrokers in business and tech reacted to the midterms results amid the blue wave sweeping across the country:
Reid Hoffman , the cofounder of LinkedIn and a Democratic megadonor, reacted to the party's big wins in a post on X Tuesday evening.
"Voters made clear they demand a different kind of country. Americans want an economy that can compete globally and deliver for them at home. And they made clear that they want leaders they can trust to fight for their constituents," he wrote.
"This night blew the doors off our expectations. From Texas to Ohio, Kentucky to Iowa, and South Carolina to Indiana, voters rejected the status quo. Tonight's lesson: Never discount any voter in any place," he continued.
Hoffman has been active in politics and vocal about his support for Democrats, spending tens of millions this election cycle. He also spent millions to support Kamala Harris's campaign in 2024.
Hoffman has previously said the Democratic Party had alienated Silicon Valley and was partly to blame for its shift to the right.
Elon Musk , who spent hundreds of millions to support Republicans, broke his silence late on election night with two short X posts.
"Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," Musk said, referencing concerns that Democratic wins could mean more scrutiny on data center development.
"Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn't work this time," he joked in a quick follow-up post.
Musk, the world's richest person, spent more money than any other individual in the midterms, donating a whopping $446 million, mostly in Texas, the state he calls home along with his companies Tesla and SpaceX.
In addition to Talarico's Senate seat, the Texas governorship was also won by a Democrat, Gina Hinojosa. It was the first time in decades a Democrat won a statewide race in the Lone Star state.
Lisa Su, the CEO of chipmaker AMD, saw the election results as showing that tech companies need to do more to convince people about the benefits of AI.
"At the end of the day, what we need to do is ensure that everybody wins from AI," she said in an interview on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street."
"I do think this is an opportunity for us as a tech industry to realize that we need to make sure that the value proposition is clear to every local community that is going to host a data center, and I believe we can do that," she added.
Dara Khosrowshahi , the CEO of Uber, shared his thoughts on the midterms in a Wednesday morning interview with CNBC.
"I think the people of our country sent a message regarding change," he said. "I think that continuous inflation really has taken a mark on the consumer."
"I think it's up to businesses and up to our politicians and leaders in Washington to respond, and I hope that they do, because it was a very clear message that was sent out."
Khorowshahi, who is Iranian by birth, was a vocal critic of Trump during his first term, but donated $1 million to the president's inaugural fund after the 2024 election.
Keith Rabois held executive roles at PayPal, LinkedIn, and Square, before becoming managing director at Khosla Ventures. As the results came in overnight, he posted on X: "Another reason to move to Miami."
It came shortly after the Associated Press called Florida's US Senate race for the Republican incumbent, Ashley Moody, who held on despite a strong Democratic swing.
While two of the city's three main congressional districts elected Democrats in huge swings, the one that covers downtown Miami looks set to narrowly reelect the Republican incumbent, with 99% of the vote counted.
Rabois is married to Jacob Helberg, Trump's undersecretary of state for economic affairs, and their wedding ceremony was officiated by Sam Altman.
Last year, The Wall Street Journal reported the couple was selling their Miami Beach home for $65 million as Helberg relocated to Washington, DC, although Rabois planned to stay based in Miami.
Brad Gerstner , CEO of Altimeter Capital, had thoughts on how the US data center buildout would be affected by the elections.
In a guest appearance on the All-In podcast livestream Tuesday evening, Gerstner said fears that a "blue tsunami" could make it difficult to build new data centers are "overblown."
But he said that election results could slow down the development of the centers, and candidates like Gina Hinojosa, the Democrat who won the Texas gubernatorial race Tuesday, could "issue a moratorium on new data centers." He said this could be "really challenging for the AI infratrade."
Gerstner also said that Republicans and the AI community have "struggled with the messaging" over AI as the affordability crisis has weighed on Americans' minds.
The investor is the architect of "Trump Accounts," the investment vehicle for children in the country that launched in July.
Dylan Patel, CEO of SemiAnalysis, hinted at what he believes a blue wave could mean for the AI buildout.
"I am now bullish space datacenters," Patel said in a post on X alongside a screenshot of results out of Texas that showed Hinojosa with an early lead over incumbent Republican Gov. Greg Abbott.
Ahead of the midterms, some in tech expressed concern that Democratic wins would mean additional scrutiny on data centers, which have faced fierce opposition in communities across the US.
Dan Ives, a veteran Wall Street analyst and AI bull, said the midterms will put the brakes on the rapid construction of data centers.
In a post on X, he said the "Democratic blue tidal wave across the Senate and House was a seismic shift that will have a negative impact on the pace of the AI Revolution buildout in the US over the next few years."
Ives added that while some investors will prefer a slower pace, others will view it as added risk.
"We estimate 10% of data centers will not happen now," he said.
Richard Branson, the billionaire founder of the Virgin Group, wrote in a post on LinkedIn that the results of the midterm election are not just "a decisive repudiation of Trump" but also an encouraging sign "about the limits of money in politics."
Branson wrote, "As a successful entrepreneur, I have felt embarrassed by the billions that tech entrepreneurs and hedge fund managers have spent on — mostly Republican — campaigns this election cycle, in an attempt to buy influence and control over public policy."
Branson added that voters looked past the "hateful and false messages" fueled by the billions spent on funding candidates, voting based on the issues that mattered to them.
"I hope this will prompt the next Congress to start a fresh conversation about the toxic impact of money in politics and the need for meaningful campaign finance reform," he wrote.

Election nights tend to rattle retirement savers, but Wall Street opened Wednesday more calmly. The SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust ( NYSEARCA:SPY ), the most widely held stand-in for the benchmark S&P 500, traded at $763.08 before the open on November 4. That was up 1.16% from its November 3 close of $754.35. Reuters reported that stocks rallied and the dollar dipped after what it called a Democratic midterm sweep. But one session tells a 401(k) holder very little. The more useful guide is how the index behaved in the weeks and months after past midterms. That record shows a steady winning run, along with a few sharp breaks.
SPY's monthly adjusted prices add dividends back in and go back to December 1999. That covers six full midterm cycles. The table compares SPY's October close just before each vote with its November close just after. The index rose in five of the six Novembers and finished flat in the sixth.

The longer view is even more consistent. The SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF Trust ( NYSEARCA:DIA ) tracks the Dow Jones Industrial Average. It finished higher in all six cycles since 2002, measured from the October close before each vote to the November close a year later. The smallest gain was 4.8% after the 2014 vote and the largest was 20.0% after 2002. In between came 13.9% after 2006, 11.2% after 2010, 14.6% after 2018, and 12.4% after 2022. That run fits a pattern we have tracked before: the year after a midterm has historically been one of the better periods of the four-year presidential cycle.
For anyone near retirement, there is a catch: even the good years came with painful setbacks. In 2018, SPY gained 1.9% in November, then fell 8.8% in December alone. It ended the year at an adjusted 222.8902, which was 7.1% below its level before the election. December also gave back most or all of November's gains in 2002 and 2022.
Even the 12-month periods that ended higher had real turbulence along the way. From November 2018 through October 2019, SPY returned 12.2%, yet at one point it sat 8.8% below its prior peak. From November 2022 through October 2023, SPY returned 4.2% and included an 8.3% drop. From November 2014 through October 2015, SPY returned just 2.4% and fell 8.5% between July and September 2015. In each of those three years, the post-midterm lift came with at least one drop of more than 8%.
This cycle starts from a higher level than most. SPY began Wednesday up 11.9% for the year and 265.9% over 10 years. Still, it went into the vote down 0.86% for the week and 0.85% for the month. A change in congressional control can reshape spending priorities, and the sectors most tied to Washington tend to adjust first, before broad index funds feel much of the shift.
Over the long run, Wall Street has tended to come out stronger after midterms. The Dow ETF's six-for-six record a year out backs that up. One of Wall Street's biggest AI bulls says the sweeping Democratic victory in the midterm elections will slow the pace of the AI data center build-out in the US over the next two years. AI-related stocks dropped on Wednesday, including Elon Musk-led SpaceX ( SPCX ) and EV maker Tesla ( TSLA ), which fell 4% before trimming losses as the rest of the market surged.
Shares of cloud provider CoreWeave ( CRWV ) and data center-related companies IREN ( IREN ) and Vertiv ( VRT ) also traded lower on Wednesday after Democrats won a majority in the House and Senate on Tuesday night and flipped governorships across key states.
"There is no way to sugarcoat that Democrats taking control, especially over the Senate, will create some major hurdles for AI and tech legislation in the Beltway over the next 2 years," Yorkville's partner and managing director, Dan Ives, wrote on Wednesday.
Those hurdles, Ives said, will slow the pace of 800 to 1,000 planned AI data centers across the US. The analyst pointed out that the biggest worry for tech investors and the AI trade is the state of Texas, where around 25%-30% of data center gigawatts and capacity will come from.
Democrat Gina Hinojosa won the Texas Governor race over incumbent Greg Abbott in a surprise result. While Abbott currently has a moratorium on data centers in Texas, the prevailing view was that it would have ended were he reelected.
"Hinojosa is a known anti-data center politician and negative on the AI buildout, which makes worries around the future of the data center buildout in Texas a real issue for tech investors," Ives said.
This poses a problem for companies like Texas-based SpaceX, which has been building out its AI infrastructure and taking steps toward a potential merger with Tesla.
"SpaceX and Musk are clearly caught front and center in this spiderweb," said Ives.
"There will be a lot of negotiations and politics on this front especially in Texas which is the foundation of the AI buildout in the US … and Big Tech will need to embrace this new political landscape as of today," he added.
"Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," Elon Musk wrote on X following the election results.
Data center concerns emerged as a key issue in the 2026 midterm elections, with candidates facing growing public opposition to proposed facility locations, the expansion of power infrastructure needed to support them, and concerns that rising electricity demand could drive up consumer costs.
One silver lining for investors may be that political headwinds will force a slowdown in AI capex. AI-related jitters have already weighed on the Tech sector ( XLK ) in recent weeks, with financing concerns hitting neocloud providers that rent out computing capacity, while semiconductor stocks have also retreated.
Long-term, however, Ives remains bullish on the AI trade, as "the Street still is way underestimating the future revenue growth and profitability" stemming from AI.
Fundstrat's Tom Lee is also largely optimistic despite the blue wave.
"President Trump exercises veto power vs any potential 'anti-AI' 'anti-data center' bills," Lee wrote in a note on Tuesday prior to the election results. He also noted that Democrats would likely embrace AI data centers because they bring money and jobs to a community.

Crude oil inventories in the United States saw a decrease of 900,000 barrels during the week ending October 30, according to new data from the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) released on Wednesday. The decrease brings commercial stockpiles to 409.8 million barrels, according to government data, which is now 4% below the five-year average for this time of year.
Total commercial petroleum inventories slipped by 8.2 million barrels during the reporting period.
The EIA’s data release follows API’s figures that were released a day earlier, which reported that crude oil inventories had fallen by 5.267 million barrels in the period.
Crude futures were trading down at 10:09 a.m. in New York. Brent futures were trading down at $100.71 per barrel—down $2.89 (-2.79%) on the day and down roughly $15 per barrel from this same time last week. WTI was also trading down on the day, by $2.79 per barrel (-2.90%) on Wednesday morning at $93.30 , down nearly $9 per barrel since this time last week.
For total motor gasoline, the EIA reported that inventories decreased by 200,000 barrels, after growing by 3.9 million barrels in the week prior. The most recent figures showed that average daily gasoline production increased to 9.7 million barrels. For middle distillates, inventories decreased by 3.6 million with production decreasing to an average of 5.2 million barrels daily. Distillate inventories are now 13% below the five-year average.
Total products supplied—a proxy for U.S. oil demand—jumped to a 4 week average of 21.2 million barrels per day over the last four weeks, up 4.2% compared to the same period last year. Gasoline demand averaged 8.6 million barrels per day over the last four weeks, with the distillate four-week average supplied at 4.2 million barrels—up 8.7% year over year.

articles.title_orig: French blood storage impacted by freezer hacks as theories swirl about culprits
articles.title_zh: French blood storage impacted by freezer hacks as theories swirl about culprits
articles.content_orig:
French authorities say that fridges used in medical facilities to store blood for donations were impacted by recent cyber-attacks by unknown hackers.
The French Blood Establishment (EFS) said cold rooms storing blood were impacted by hackers, with temperatures set to rise - but staff intervened to protect blood supplies.
"No health impact has been identified and no loss of blood products is to be reported," the EFS said.
Up until now, only supermarkets were known to have been impacted by the hacks.
Meanwhile rumours have been circulating online about Russian hacktivist groups claiming they worked together to hack one of the systems that was used in the attacks which have affected European supermarkets.
Noname057(16) and Z-Pentest Alliance posted that they successfully hacked Danfoss which led to speculation that they were the culprits behind the freezer hacks.
But analysts now question whether or not that meant they were behind the supermarket cyber-attacks.
While Russian groups are not being ruled out, experts say Iranian hacktivists or nation state hackers - or even teenagers pulling pranks - could also be the culprits.
Cyber-security researchers at multiple firms are poring over evidence gathered from so-called "honeypots" to provide clues as to who is behind the waves of freezer hacks.
Three separate cyber-security firms have deployed fake freezer software traps to monitor how hackers attempt to use them for attacks.
In cyber-security, a "honeypot" is a digital decoy - such as a fake computer network or file - deliberately set up to look like a vulnerable target to lure and trap hackers.
By monitoring these traps, security experts can safely study an attacker's methods without putting real systems at risk.
According to activity gathered after the first wave of cyber-attacks, the second wave which hit several European countries was highly targeted.
"The fact that all these fridge freezers were hit simultaneously suggests planning and coordination," says Ryan Dewhurst from Spanish cyber-security company Previdian.
The entry point to the affected freezer software products was not difficult to exploit as they were poorly protected, with known attack methods already floating around online.
But experts like Dewhurst say the hacker or hackers had to gather the information about the devices' public IP addresses to create a target list then take time to plan which methods to use and when to execute them.
"Given the reported timing of when the devices had their temperatures increased, which seems to have been overnight for maximum damage - this is further evidence that the attack was planned and co-ordinated," he said.
Another cyber firm which has deployed similar honeypot tech to lure the hackers into revealing their tactics is Strathclyde-based Lupovis.
It had honeypots which appeared to be located around the world, and started seeing activity 10 days before the second wave of cyber-attacks.
Intriguingly, the team saw hackers scanning and probing their fake freezer sites only in Europe.
"We saw none of our honeypots in places like Africa or South America targeted at all," said Lupovis founder Dr Xavier Bellekens.
"Even pots in Ukraine were left alone."
A third company - French cyber-defence firm Sekoia - also noticed scanning activity prior to the second wave of cyber-attacks, but said it could have been automatic scanning without malicious intent.
In a report to its customers, it said evidence suggested the nature of the attack aligned with activity of Russian hacktivists or the Russian government, which is being accused of carrying out so-called "hybrid warfare" cyber-attacks across Europe.
But Sekoia's research also points to Iranian regime hackers or hacktivists too.
"Iranian-aligned actors have an established record of targeting internet-exposed industrial control systems and previous incidents involved the same equipment in Israel and the US - both adversaries of Iran," the report said.
According to Sekoia, about 40 Israeli supermarkets running Danfoss controllers were compromised back in 2022.
Meanwhile in late August, freezers in at least six US military bases were forced into defrost mode, as in France. The controller models remain unconfirmed and investigations are ongoing.
"To date, we have no technical evidence indicating the involvement of Russian-speaking groups," a Sekoia spokesperson told the BBC.
"Furthermore, as NoName057 is not known to effectively conduct operations beyond DDoS attacks and has a history of making false attributions, we remain sceptical of their alleged claim of responsibility."
Distributed denial of service (DDoS) attacks work by flooding a website or online service with internet traffic in an attempt to throw it offline, or otherwise make it inaccessible.
Authorities in several countries are actively investigating the hacks and warning supermarkets about potential future attacks.
But no formal attribution has been made.
None of the three cyber firms which have been gathering honey pot data are ruling out that it could be a teenager.
But with the degree of planning necessary the experts all agree it would have to be a well co-ordinated group - and if so, they would expect online bragging to surface soon.
Sekoia also said the possibility remains that all three waves could have been carried out by different and distinct groups or copycats.
